en: Preface to the Eighth Assembly of the Mahāprajñāpāramitā Sūtra:
The Section on Nāgaśrī, composed by the Śramaṇa Xuánzé of Xímíng Monastery.
I record that when the external is cleansed according to pure regulations, the inner spirit is illuminated; when the divine principle is tranquil within, it suddenly transcends.
When manifesting in worldly activities, if one does not examine the interplay between movement and stillness, one may err by either following or resisting them.

Therefore, Master Miaoxiang adopted the principles of Śrāvastī, while Master Longxiang followed the regulations of Rājagṛha. They lowered their steps and circled around, adjusting their postures and raising their hands; they contemplated through non-contemplation and proceeded through non-proceeding. Consuming illusory food, they resembled hanging gourds;
utilizing the non-utilizable, they were like drawing from a cold well.

Suddenly, he let loose his gaze upon the arts of the void and clarified his breast in ocean-like stillness; he nurtured living beings as the essence of the water-nature and exhausted all merit as a treasury of jewels. He remained tranquil amidst the six stirrings without wavering, and brought the three vehicles to their ultimate station. Having no ruler yet not failing to rule, he set aside the sovereign mind to manifest clearly;
having no kin yet not failing to be kin, he expanded the circle of virtuous friends to gather them from afar.
This causes the lay devotee to take up the alms bowl, startled that his long arms no longer exist;
it causes the Arhat to cast aside his robe, stunned as he feels his heart has already perished.
It is like a mirage of a sea palace: one knows it is but accumulated vapors and thus forgets the effort of climbing toward it.
The phoenix mirror contains its beauty; realizing that all is but emptiness, one ceases to grasp at it.

Thus, one can reflect upon the distant from what is near, and establish the conventional based on the ultimate truth. One recognizes that life is as precarious as dew gathering on a blade of grass, and knows that this illusory body is as fleeting as a bubble floating on water. Like lightning, the luster of purple and blue robes vanishes in an instant; like clouds, the shadows of carriages and canopies dissolve into the void.

The phrasing is concise yet the principles are comprehensive; what was formerly secret is now transmitted. Although this single fascicle is a solitary translation, upon repeated reading, its manifold flavors are indeed profound.
Translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Xuanzang by Imperial Decree. Chapter Eight: The Section on Nāgaśrī. Thus have I heard:
At one time, the Bhagavat was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park, proclaiming the True Dharma for the great assembly.
At that time, the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Mañjuśrī, having dressed in the early part of the day and taken up his bowl, was gradually proceeding toward the city of Śrāvastī.
Then, there was a bodhisattva named Nāgaśrī who, seeing him, asked:
"Venerable sir, where are you going?"
Mañjuśrī said:

"I wish to enter this city of Śrāvastī to wander for alms, for the sake of benefiting and bringing happiness to many sentient beings, out of compassion for the great multitude of beings in the world, and for the benefit, welfare, and peace of gods and humans."
Nāgaśrī replied: "Indeed,
Venerable One!"
"Have you still not yet broken through the perception of food?
Mañjuśrī replied, "I do not perceive the existence of the perception of food at all; what, then, could there be to break?"
Why is this? Because all dharmas are by nature empty and quiescent, like space, neither subject to destruction nor interruption; how could I possibly destroy them?
Neither the devas, Māras, or Brahmās, nor the śramaṇas and brāhmaṇas of the world, can destroy them either.
Why is this so? Because the self-nature of all phenomena is equal to the realm of empty space; they are ultimately and entirely empty, immovable, and incapable of being destroyed.
Furthermore, all phenomena are like the great void; no sentient beings—whether devas, māras, Brahmās, śramaṇas, or others—are able to grasp or possess them.
"Why is this? Because all phenomena are by nature remote, they cannot be grasped. Nāgaśrī said:
"If it is as you have said, how does a bodhisattva engage in battle and contention with Māra?

Mañjuśrī replied, "A bodhisattva never engages in battle and contention by striking the great drums of Māra's army; at that time, the bodhisattva likewise perceives not even the slightest reality among phenomena upon which to rely for entering meditative absorption."
Why is this? Because although the Bodhisattva sees them beating drums and the like, he feels no fear.
It is like a magician who conjures up enemies through illusion; though they appear to cause distress, he does not give rise to fear.
In this way, when a bodhisattva knows that the nature of phenomena is empty and entirely like an illusion, they have no fear whatsoever.

If at any time a bodhisattva were to experience fear, they would not be worthy of being venerated by gods, humans, and others; however, because bodhisattvas understand emptiness and are without fear, they are capable of serving as a truly pure field of merit for all beings.
Nāgaśrī asked, "Is there anyone capable of realizing bodhi?
Mañjuśrī replied:
"There is indeed one who can testify.
Nāgabhadra asked, "Who is the witness?"
Mañjuśrī said: "If there were no names, designations, or linguistic conventions, that would be capable of realization.
Nāgaśrī replied:
"If that is so, how can he realize it?
Mañjuśrī replied, "His mind is unborn;

he does not conceptualize awakening or the seat of awakening, nor does he take pity upon sentient beings. By means of a mind without representation and a mind without vision, he is able to realize unsurpassed, perfect, and complete awakening."
Nāgaśrī said: "If that is so, with what kind of mind, etc., will the Venerable One attain bodhi?
Mañjuśrī replied:
“I have no destination, nor am I one who goes; I have nothing at all to learn.
It is not that I shall go in the future to the Bodhi tree, sit upon the Vajra-seat, realize Great Enlightenment, and turn the wondrous Wheel of Dharma to deliver beings from birth and death.”
Why is this? All phenomena are immovable, indestructible, ungraspable, and ultimately empty and quiescent.
By means of such a mind that does not proceed toward anything, I shall attain bodhi.

Nāgaśrī said: "The Venerable One’s words are all based on the ultimate truth (paramārtha), causing all sentient beings to have faith and understanding in this Dharma so that they may be liberated from afflictions.
If sentient beings are liberated from their afflictions, they will be able to utterly destroy the snare-net of Māra."
Mañjuśrī said:
"The snare-net of Māra cannot be destroyed. Why is this so?
"Māra is a synonym for bodhi. Why is this?
Because both Māra and his armies are by nature non-existent and utterly unfindable; therefore, I say that Māra is no different from a synonym for bodhi."
Nāgaśrī asked: "What is meant by 'bodhi'?
Mañjuśrī replied:
"What is called 'bodhi' pervades all phenomena across all times and places.

Just as space is entirely without obstruction and exists everywhere throughout time, place, and phenomena, so too is bodhi; because it is without obstruction, it pervades all times, places, and phenomena."
"Such enlightenment is most supreme; what kind of enlightenment do you now wish to realize, O Noble One?
Nāgaśrī replied, "I wish to realize the unsurpassed."
Mañjuśrī said: "You should desist now!
Unsurpassed enlightenment is not a dharma that can be realized; for you to wish to realize it is to engage in conceptual proliferation."
Why is this? Unsurpassed Bodhi is free from characteristics and is quiescent; for you to now desire to grasp it would constitute frivolous conceptual proliferation (*prapañca*).
It is, for example, as if someone were to say this:

"I shall cause an illusory being to sit upon the seat of enlightenment and realize illusory, unsurpassed, perfect, and complete awakening"—such words are utterly frivolous and conceptual proliferation;
for since even an illusory being cannot be found, how could one possibly cause such a being to realize illusory great awakening!
Illusion, with respect to illusory phenomena, is neither joined nor dispersed; it is without grasping and without relinquishing, for its intrinsic nature is empty in both cases.

The Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, have taught that all phenomena are beyond conceptual differentiation and are all like illusory events. Now that you wish to realize unsurpassed bodhi, would this not simply result in your differentiating illusory phenomena?
However, all phenomena are neither to be grasped nor to be abandoned; they are neither produced nor destroyed.
A non-existent phenomenon cannot effect the creation or destruction of a phenomenon, and a non-existent phenomenon cannot bring about the conjunction or separation of a phenomenon.
Why is this so? Because all dharmas are neither joined nor dispersed;

their self-nature is entirely empty, free from "self" and "what belongs to self," equal to the realm of space. They cannot be spoken or shown, cannot be praised or disparaged, have no high or low, and involve neither loss nor gain. They are inconceivable and beyond frivolous proliferation; their fundamental nature is void and still, being ultimately empty like an illusion or a dream. Being without counterpart and without peer, how could one possibly give rise to a mind of discrimination toward them?
Nāgaśrī said: "Excellent,
Venerable One!"
"I have now attained enlightenment by means of this very concentration.
Why is this? It is because the Honored One has expounded the profound Dharma for me. Mañjuśrī said:
"Up until now, I have never proclaimed to you anything—whether manifest or secret, profound or shallow—so how could I enable you to attain bodhi?"

Why is this? Because the intrinsic nature of all phenomena is ultimately inexpressible. Your claim that I am teaching a profound Dharma is merely the practice of conceptual proliferation (*prapañca*);
yet in truth, I am not one who can teach the Dharma, for the intrinsic nature of all phenomena is likewise inexpressible.
Suppose someone were to say:

"I am able to analyze and explain the characteristics of the consciousness of an illusory person, asserting that the consciousness of such illusory persons possesses this or that specific distinction.
By making such a statement, he contradicts his own true words.
Why is this? For even an illusory person is not something that can be cognized, much less a characteristic of cognition!
Your current claim that I am preaching a profound Dharma to enable you to realize unsurpassed bodhi is likewise so.
"Since all dharmas are like illusory phenomena, their ultimate emptiness cannot even be known, let alone be proclaimed!
At that time, the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva Aparājita came to where he was, and having heard this, praised him, saying:
"Excellent! "
Excellent!
O Righteous One!
O Great Being!
"are able to engage in debate regarding this profound Dharma-gate.
At that time, Mañjuśrī questioned Ajita, saying:
"Noble being, Great Being, what Dharma do you teach?"
Now, a bodhisattva does not form this thought:
"I am a bodhisattva, a true being, a great being, who is able to preach the profound Dharma for the sake of sentient beings.
To form such a thought is to engage in conceptual proliferation (*prapañca*).
Furthermore, Ajita!

Is there any such thing as an echo that exists by way of its own intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) and is truly capable of producing speech, thereby giving rise to the consciousness of a listener that designates various phenomena?
At that time, Ajita replied:
"No," said Mañjuśrī, "in this way all phenomena are entirely unreal;

they are like echoes, without name, without characteristic, and without anything to be grasped or clung to. To have attachment to these is to engage in conceptual proliferation (*prapañca*), and if one engages in conceptual proliferation, one wanders through birth and death."

Failing to understand all phenomena as being like echoes, they give rise to disputes; because disputes arise, the mind wavers; when the mind wavers, many errors and delusions occur; and as these delusions increase, one wanders through the cycle of the various realms of existence.
Therefore, the World-Honored One personally instructed and exhorted the bhikṣus day and night, saying:

"O bhikṣus, do not engage in frivolous discourse. Within this Dharma of cessation taught by me, you should constantly contemplate, carefully examine, and diligently cultivate the patience regarding the non-attainment of dharmas."
Thus the Great Holy Dharma-King Śāntamati spoke: "All dharmas are empty, their original nature is quiescent, without defilement, without attainment, and without any basis for abiding.
One who can know this as it truly is shall be liberated from birth and death and will certainly realize bodhi and nirvāṇa."
Then, having heard these words, Nāgaśrī immediately asked Mañjuśrī again:
"Venerable One, from what cycle of birth and death have you been liberated?"
Mañjuśrī said: "Virtuous one, from what birth-and-death do you say the Tathāgata has attained liberation?
The World-Honored One, Possessor of the Ten Powers, constantly teaches that the past, future, and present constitute the phenomena of birth-and-death."
Nāgaśrī said: “World-Honored One!

Have you not taught that all phenomena are like illusions and transformations? If this is so, sentient beings should have already realized unsurpassed bodhi from the very beginning; how then could there be birth and death?”
"Why is this? Venerable sir, you too have said that all phenomena are not real and are entirely like illusions and transformations.
Mañjuśrī replied:

"Since the distant past, I have never proclaimed the nature and characteristics of phenomena (*dharmatā-lakṣaṇa*), nor have I differentiated them, grasped them, or engaged in their fabrication. Why is this?
Because the nature and characteristics of all phenomena cannot be indicated, cannot be differentiated, cannot be grasped, and cannot be fabricated."

"If all sentient beings were able to realize, as it truly is, that all phenomena are like illusions and transformations, they would have already attained unsurpassed enlightenment from the very beginning.

However, because sentient beings cannot thoroughly penetrate the fact that all phenomena are like illusions and transformations, they wander in the cycle of birth and death through the various realms of existence."

Just as a master illusionist, depending upon various materials, conjures through illusion all manner of illusory phenomena—namely, the worldly hosts of devas, māras, brahmās, Śakras, śramaṇas, brahmins, nāgas, yakṣas, asuras, and other human and non-human beings—the deluded masses cling to these as being truly existent; yet the wise illusionist knows they lack any real nature and that there is nothing but the manifestation of various false appearances.

Although all these phenomena are like illusions and transformations, sentient beings, out of ignorance and lack of understanding, perceive what does not exist as existing and conceive the impermanent as permanent. Within these phenomena, they engage in various conceptual discriminations—discriminating between form and mind, the conditioned and the unconditioned, the tainted and the untainted, and so forth. Because of these discriminations, they do not know phenomena as they truly are, that they are all like illusions and transformations; and because of this lack of knowledge, they wander through the cycle of birth and death.
If all sentient beings were to understand all phenomena as they truly are—like illusions and transformations—then the Buddha-dharma would no longer increase. Why is this so?
All classes of sentient beings have possessed from the beginning all the sublime dharmas of the Buddhas; for they never retreat from the Buddha-wisdom.

All sentient beings can be established in the unshakable awakened wisdom of the sublime dharmas of the Buddhas. They know that the nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*) is empty—without name, without mark, without support, without abiding, without grasping, without clinging, unobstructed, and unattached—just like space. It is without the *ālayavijñāna* and without the *ninyati*; it is supreme tranquility and ultimate stillness; it is without arising and without ceasing, without defilement and without purity, without formation and without destruction, neither existent nor non-existent.
By means of this, one achieves profound patience therein and never remains distant from the sublime Dharma of the Buddhas.

Why is this so? Because the sublime Dharma of the Buddhas is devoid of intrinsic nature and devoid of characteristics; it cannot be established, cannot be proclaimed, and cannot be indicated, pervading all classes of sentient beings like space.
At that time, Nāgaśrī, having heard this profound Dharma, was filled with joy and exultation, and he praised Mañjuśrī:
“Excellent! Excellent!”

"What the Venerable One has spoken is profoundly deep, subtle, and inconceivable; that all sentient beings are never separated from the sublime Dharma of the Buddhas—who could believe and understand this?"
Mañjuśrī replied:

“The true sons of all Buddhas are all able to believe and understand; that is to say, those who follow by faith, those who follow the Dharma, the eighth-rank practitioners, stream-enterers, once-returners, non-returners, arhats, pratyekabuddhas, and bodhisattvas who have attained the stage of non-retrogression—those who are unshakable and unswerving regarding all pure dharmas, and who are well-established in the dharma of ultimate emptiness and the dharma of non-apprehension—are able to believe and understand with deep conviction.”

Why is this? Because these bodhisattvas have already brought the sublime seat of awakening before them and are able to let out the great lion’s roar before the world—including its gods, Māras, Brahmās, Śakras, śramaṇas, brahmins, asuras, and others, both human and non-human—saying:
"Seated cross-legged upon this seat, until I have attained unsurpassed awakening, I shall never at any time during the interval break this posture."
Why is this? Because these bodhisattvas have already well established themselves in the dharma of ultimate emptiness and the dharma of non-apprehension, and thus cannot be moved.
It is, for example, like a royal pillar that is extremely well-settled and firm, which even the lords of oxen cannot shake.

Thus, when a bodhisattva is well-established in the dharma of ultimate emptiness and the dharma of non-apprehension, no sentient beings can cause them to waver or lead them away from their state of awareness and its objects, nor from the seat of enlightenment.
Nāgaśrī asked: "What is meant by 'the place of awakening' and 'the place of the seat of enlightenment'?
Then, Mañjuśrī questioned him in return:
"What is meant by the Tathāgata’s transformation?
What is the locus of the Tathāgata’s transformation?
And what is the basis upon which the Tathāgata’s transformation relies?"
"What is the Tathāgata’s manifested realization of the Dharma, by virtue of which it is said that the Tathāgata manifests the teaching of the Dharma through transformation? Nāgaśrī replied:

"I do not even perceive a real Tathāgata; how much less could I perceive a Tathāgata’s transformation, the locus of transformation, the basis of transformation, or the manifested realization of the Dharma, by means of which one could say that the Tathāgata manifests the teaching of the Dharma through transformation?"
Mañjuśrī said: “Excellent! Excellent!”

What you have said regarding that which is taught and that which is known is most consistent with reason; for you have already given rise to the patient acceptance (*kṣānti*) of non-apprehension regarding all phenomena (*anupalambha*) and are thus able to speak in this way. You should know that the same applies to the awakening and that which is awakened, and so forth.
Nāgaśrī said: "The patient acceptance of the non-apprehension of all phenomena has neither arising nor destruction. Why is this so?
Since all phenomena are empty and lack intrinsic nature, their own characteristics are also empty.
Thus, these phenomena are signless, non-oppositional, formless, and invisible, equal to space; how then can one give rise to the patient acceptance of the non-apprehension of all phenomena?

If the patience regarding the non-apprehension of all phenomena had the sense of being something that could arise, then the patience regarding echoes, the patience regarding reflections, the patience regarding masses of foam, the patience regarding bubbles, the patience regarding mirages, the patience regarding plantain trees, the patience regarding illusions, the patience regarding dreams, the patience regarding transformations, the patience regarding mirror-images, the patience regarding gandharva-cities, and the patience regarding the realm of space would likewise have the sense of arising.
Why is this? It is because it is impossible for the patience equal to space (ākāśasama-kṣānti) to have the sense of arising.

If a bodhisattva mahāsattva, upon hearing such a teaching, is not startled, not terrified, without confusion, without doubt, and their mind does not sink, this is precisely the bodhisattva’s supreme patience toward dharmas (anuttara-dharma-kṣānti).
Mañjuśrī said: "Since the various assemblies of bodhisattvas have not attained the patience of non-attainment (*anupalambha-kṣānti*), how could there be no distinctions among them?
Nāgaśrī replied:
"If a bodhisattva assembly has attachment to even a small portion of phenomena, this is called practicing with something to be attained.
If various bodhisattvas should think:
'I am fully able to understand and comprehend the profound.'"
This is called practicing with the attainment of something.
If various bodhisattvas should think:
"I am one who has accomplished profound patience," [they are practicing with attainment].
"This is what is called practicing with the notion of attainment.
If bodhisattvas should think: 'I am able to fully believe and accept the profound [teachings],' [they are likewise practicing with attainment]."
"This is what is called practicing with the attainment of something.
If various bodhisattvas should form this thought:
'I am fully able to understand and comprehend all meanings.'"
"This is what is called practicing with the attainment of something.
If various bodhisattvas form this thought:
'I am able to fully awaken to and comprehend all dharmas.'"
"This is what is called practicing with the notion of attainment.
If bodhisattvas should think:
'I am able to understand the intrinsic nature of all phenomena.'"
This is what is called practicing with the attainment of something.
If bodhisattvas should think:
"I am able to practice the bodhisattva path," [they are practicing with attainment].
"This is what is called practicing with the attainment of something.
If various bodhisattvas should think:
'I am able to adorn and purify various buddha-fields.'"
"This is what is called practicing with the notion of attainment.
If a bodhisattva should think:
'I am able to bring sentient beings to maturity.'"
This is what is called practicing with the attainment of something.
If various bodhisattvas should form this thought:
"I shall certainly realize awakening."
"This is what is called practicing with the attainment of something.
If a bodhisattva should think:
'I am certainly able to turn the unsurpassed wheel of Dharma.'"
"This is what is called practicing with the notion of attainment.
If bodhisattvas should think:
'I am able to rescue and deliver all classes of sentient beings.'"
This is what is called practicing with the attainment of something.
If various bodhisattvas should form such thoughts as:
"I have something to practice; I have something to realize."
This is what is called practicing with the apprehension of something to be attained.
If various bodhisattvas should form this thought:
"I am able to practice the perfection of generosity, ethical discipline, patience, diligence, meditative concentration, and wisdom."
This is what is called practicing with the attainment of something.
If bodhisattvas should think:
"I am able to practice the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment, such as the four foundations of mindfulness," [they are practicing with attainment].
"This is what is called practicing with the apprehension of something to be attained.
If various bodhisattvas should form this thought:
'I am able to practice the meditative concentrations (dhyāna), the immeasurables (apramāṇa), the samādhis, the meditative attainments (samāpatti), and the doors of dhāraṇī.'"
"This is what is called practicing with the notion of attainment.
If various bodhisattvas should think:

'I am able to approach and realize the Tathāgata’s ten powers, the four fearlessnesses, the four unhindered understandings, great loving-kindness, great compassion, great sympathetic joy, and great equanimity, as well as the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha and other such immeasurable and boundless sublime dharmas of the Buddhas.'"
"This is what is called practicing with something to be attained.
Because a bodhisattva does not practice with anything to be attained, there is no distinction in the patience regarding the non-attainment of dharmas. Mañjuśrī said:
“If that is so, how does a bodhisattva train in the practice that leads to enlightenment? Nāgaśrī replied,
“If the assembly of bodhisattvas has no grasping or attachment toward any phenomena, this is training in the practice that leads to enlightenment.”
If the assembly of bodhisattvas has nothing upon which to rely among all phenomena, this is training in the practice that leads to awakening;

if the assembly of bodhisattvas directly realizes that all phenomena depend on various conditions, are empty and devoid of intrinsic nature, and are free from self and what belongs to a self, this is training in the practice that leads to awakening;
if the assembly of bodhisattvas, though they engage in activity, have no conceptualization of activity, this is training in the practice that leads to awakening.
Mañjuśrī said: “So it is! So it is!”
It is exactly as you have said.

For example, though a person in a dream may claim to travel to or dwell in various places, there is no going, coming, walking, standing, sitting, or lying down; nor is there any real place where they travel or dwell.

The Bodhisattva is likewise: although dwelling in the state of wakefulness, they engage in spiritual practice without the conceptualization of practicing; they contemplate that the intrinsic nature of all practiced deeds is empty, remaining without grasping or attachment toward any phenomena. They realize that all phenomena are without form, without marks, without the ālayavijñāna, and without nidāna, being equal to space and empty and quiescent by their very nature.

If bodhisattvas can practice in this way—without grasping and free from all conceptual proliferation—they are the true and pure field of merit for gods, humans, and others, and are worthy of receiving the world’s respect and offerings.
At that time, having heard these words, the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Nāgaśrī leaped for joy and spoke thus: “So be it!”
“Venerable One!
I now wish to go to the city of Śrāvastī to wander for alms for the sake of sentient beings.
Mañjuśrī said:

"Go as you please; however, while walking, do not lift your feet, do not set them down; do not bend or extend them; do not give rise to the mind, do not engage in conceptual proliferation; do not conceive thoughts of a path; do not conceive thoughts of cities, towns, or villages; do not conceive thoughts of small or large, male or female; and do not conceive thoughts of streets, alleys, gardens, groves, houses, doors, windows, or the like."

Why is this so? Because bodhi is far removed from all conceptualizations; it is without high or low, without contraction or expansion; the mind is stilled of all agitation, speech is free from frivolous proliferation, and it is beyond measure or number—this is the bodhi toward which a bodhisattva proceeds.
"O Benevolent One, if you can now practice in this manner, you may go wherever you wish to beg for alms.
At that time, Nāgaśrī, having received these instructions and admonitions, entered the ocean-like samādhi through its power.
For example, the great ocean has water that is vast and deep, filled to the brim and serene, abounding in all manner of precious gems, and nurturing various species of aquatic life.

In the same way, the power of this meditative concentration is vast and deep, its divine efficacy is inconceivable, and the three karmas are tranquil; it possesses the jewels of merit and sustains all sentient beings.

At that time, there was a bodhisattva named Suvicintita. Desiring to cause him to emerge quickly from his meditative absorption, he applied a great effort to stir his body; yet, although the mountains and the great earth of the trichiliocosm shook in six ways, the dragon Śrīgarbha remained in tranquil stillness of body and mind, as immovable as Mount Sumeru.
Why is this? Because by means of this meditative concentration, he causes his body, speech, and mind to abide in immovability.
Later, arising from that concentration, he rained down various fragrant flowers, bowed with palms joined toward Jetavana Grove, and with sincere reverence spoke these words:

"I take refuge in the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha; that which he has realized and taught is all most profound—its intrinsic nature is empty, untainted, and unattainable—and it enables those who hear it to attain this supreme samādhi."
The Bodhisattva Sucintita then asked him:
"Virtuous one, while you were in meditative concentration, did you perceive the earth shaking? Nāgaśrī replied:
“Sudhi, you should know this!
If there were movement or shifting within the body and mind, one would perceive the great earth and other things as also tilting and shaking.

The Buddhas, World-Honored Ones, non-retrogressive Bodhisattvas, Great Pratyekabuddhas, and Great Arhats possess bodies and minds that are tranquil and free from agitation; among all phenomena, they neither see nor perceive any movement, shifting, tilting, or shaking.”

Why is this so? Because they constantly abide in the unmoving, non-rotating, and unswaying dharmas—namely, emptiness (*śūnyatā*), signlessness (*animitta*), wishlessness (*apraṇihita*), and tranquility—and by realizing that their characteristics are fundamentally empty and their nature is the dharma of detachment, their body and mind remain unmoved by abiding in these dharmas.
At that time, having seen and heard this, Mañjuśrī rejoiced and praised Nāgaśrī, saying:
"Excellent! Excellent!"
"Since this matter has been accomplished, you may now enter the city at your pleasure to beg for alms.
Nāgaśrī replied, "I have now realized the supreme Dharma-food through the ocean-like meditative concentration; I no longer seek after material food."

I now seek only the perfections of generosity, ethical discipline, patience, diligence, meditative concentration, wisdom, skillful means, sublime aspiration, power, and knowledge, as well as other boundless bodhisattva practices, so that I may swiftly realize unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment, turn the sublime wheel of Dharma, and extract sentient beings from the great suffering of birth and death, establishing them in ultimate, pure nirvāṇa.
Now, joyfully seeking to abandon all conditioned formations (*saṃskāra*), I have no desire to nourish this defiled body and mind.

By the power of your compassion, O Venerable One, my true and pure spiritual friend (*kalyāṇamitra*), I have realized this supreme meditative concentration (*samādhi*). I now prostrate to you, the Auspiciousness of Excellence, the Boundless Auspiciousness, the Valiant Auspiciousness, the Vast Auspiciousness, the Auspiciousness of the Sublime Dharma, the Auspiciousness of Supreme Wisdom, the Inconceivable Auspiciousness, the Great Sage, the Spiritual Friend, the True and Pure Spiritual Friend.
Mañjuśrī said: "Excellent,
O worthy one!"

One is able to attain such a supreme meditative concentration comparable to the ocean, thoroughly comprehending that all phenomena are like echoes, like reflections, like dreams, like illusions, like mirages, like shadows, like magical transformations, and like cities of Gandharvas.

You should now seek the Tathāgata’s ten powers, four fearlessnesses, four analytical knowledges, great loving-kindness, great compassion, great joy, and great equanimity, as well as the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha and other immeasurable, boundless, and unsurpassed dharma-foods, to nourish and benefit yourself and your liberation-body.
All Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Samyaksaṃbuddhas subsist upon this food, enabling them to remain for immeasurable, innumerable, boundless, and inconceivable kalpas as numerous as the sands of the Ganges.
Why is this so? Such food of the Dharma is untainted and unconditioned;

it can bring about eternal liberation from attachment to worldly dharmas that do not lead to transcendence, and it can also eternally extinguish all arrogance. It is without *ālaya*, without *nnyan thos* (śrāvaka), and free from all conceptual proliferation (*prapañca*), being by nature empty and quiescent.
"All the assemblies of Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas long for this food; you too should seek it, and not seek the inferior worldly food of dharmas.
Nāgaśrī said: "I am already fully satisfied by merely hearing the praise of such unsurpassed food of dharmas as the Honored One has extolled, let alone actually obtaining it!"
If, in the future, I should obtain this food of the Dharma, I shall use the very absence of food as my skillful means to satisfy myself, and thereafter sustain all sentient beings.
Mañjuśrī said:
"Are you able to fill the realm of empty space?
He replied:
"No," said Mañjuśrī, "are you able to satisfy an echo,
a reflection, a dream, a mirage, a shadow, a light, various emanations, or a city of Gandharvas?"
He replied, “I cannot! Mañjuśrī said:
“Could you possibly satisfy all the great oceans with the various streams?
He replied, “I could not!”
Mañjuśrī said: "All phenomena are likewise so; how can you wish to satisfy them all?

If you wish for all things to be satisfied, you would be wishing to satisfy the realm of empty space, as well as echoes, reflections, dreams, and the like; you would wish to satisfy all great oceans; you would wish to satisfy the emptiness, signlessness, wishlessness, non-formation, non-action, non-arising, and non-ceasing of all phenomena; you would wish to satisfy remoteness, tranquility, detachment, nirvāṇa, the ultimate, and liberation; and you would wish to satisfy the ineffable, invisible, non-obstructive, single-characteristic True Suchness (tathatā) and Dharma-realm (dharmadhātu), which are equal to space and cannot be grasped."
Nāgaśrī said: "If, as the Honored One has stated, both food and the eater are entirely empty, then all sentient beings should have no need for sustenance.
Mañjuśrī replied:
"So it is! So it is! All sentient beings do not subsist on food."
"Suppose the Buddha were to manifest as sentient beings as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, all of whom required food; whom would you have create that much food?
Nāgaśrī replied, "A manifestation has no need for food; why bother creating it?"
Mañjuśrī said: “Phenomena and sentient beings are all like magical illusions; therefore, there is nothing that serves as sustenance for them.

If sentient beings cannot, in accordance with reality, realize that all phenomena are like magical illusions, they will falsely grasp at the various realms of birth and death within saṃsāra as having something that sustains them, yet such sustenance is ultimately unattainable.”
When one observes phenomena and sentient beings as they truly are—seeing that their intrinsic nature is empty and lacks even the slightest reality—then one finds no sustenance or support in any food.
Nāgaśrī said: “I now wish to dwell in the severance of hunger and thirst.”
Mañjuśrī said: "Since even hunger and thirst do not exist, how could there be anything that can be severed?
It is like a phantom person who speaks these words:"
"I now wish to seek water within a mirage to eliminate my hunger and thirst.
You are just like this now. Why is that?
Since all phenomena are like mirages and all sentient beings are like illusory figures, how can one wish to abide in the elimination of hunger and thirst?

Within the phenomena produced by false discrimination, neither the agent of elimination nor the object to be eliminated can be found; since hunger and thirst do not exist, who is there to perform the elimination?
All phenomena (*dharmas*) are from the very beginning sufficient in their intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*), entirely devoid of hunger and thirst;
what, then, is there to be eliminated or severed? Fools do not know this as it truly is, and thus they say, "I am hungry and thirsty, and I seek to eliminate and sever it.

Those who possess wisdom can know as it truly is that hunger and thirst are fundamentally non-existent and thus do not seek to eliminate them. Being able to thoroughly penetrate the emptiness of the nature of all phenomena, they no longer transmigrate through the various realms of birth and death. Having distanced themselves from conceptual proliferation (*prapañca*) and being without discrimination, they abide in all phenomena with nowhere to abide. Without dependence, without defilement, without entering, and without exiting, they are ultimately liberated, and discrimination is forever absent.
Nāgaśrī said: “Just as the Venerable One has spoken these essentials of all dharmas, so too does the dharma-realm manifest. Mañjuśrī said:
“The true dharma-realm (dharmadhātu) has no emergence or disappearance, no contraction or expansion. Why is this? The true dharma-realm is free from marks and profoundly tranquil;

it neither emerges nor disappears. It is beyond conceptual differentiation and beyond frivolous discourse; it is without dependence and without abiding; it is without grasping and without relinquishing; it is without movement and without transformation; it is without defilement and without purity.”

Just as the realm of space is without movement or transition, without grasping or relinquishing, without dependence or abiding, and is beyond frivolous discourse and conceptual differentiation, being neither arising nor ceasing;
so too are all phenomena: their own-characteristics are fundamentally empty, their nature is not existent, and their marks are unobtainable.
If the characteristics of phenomena were obtainable, then a Buddha who has already entered parinirvāṇa would be obtainable.
All phenomena are without the ālayavijñāna, without the nidāna; they are formless, invisible, non-obstructive, and signless, being quiescent from the very beginning.

Therefore, although as many Buddhas as there are sands in the Ganges have already entered parinirvāṇa, not a single dharma has ceased—meaning that there is no cessation of the aggregate of form, nor cessation of the aggregates of feeling, perception, mental formations, or consciousness;
likewise, there is no cessation of the sense-base of the eye, nor cessation of the sense-bases of the ear, nose, tongue, body, or mind; and there is no cessation of the sense-base of forms, nor...
The spheres of sound, odor, taste, tangibles, and mental phenomena cease;

likewise, there is no cessation of the eye-element, nor of the ear, nose, tongue, body, or mind-elements; nor is there cessation of the form-element, nor of the elements of sound, odor, taste, tangibles, or mental phenomena;
nor is there cessation of the eye-consciousness-element, nor of the ear, nose, tongue... [consciousness-elements].
There is the cessation of the body and the mental consciousness element; furthermore, there is no cessation of eye-contact, nor of ear, nose, tongue, body, or mind-contact;

furthermore, there is no cessation of the various feelings produced with eye-contact as condition, nor of the various feelings produced with ear, nose, tongue, body, or mind-contact as condition; furthermore, there is no earth element.
There is the cessation of the element of water, fire, wind, space, and consciousness.
Thus, although all Buddhas enter parinirvāṇa, not a single dharma enters parinirvāṇa.
Those who wish for dharmas to cease at the stage of parinirvāṇa are effectively wishing for the realm of great empty space to also cease at that stage. Why is this?
The nature of all phenomena is originally quiescent, inherently tranquil, and utterly still; it cannot be further extinguished.
"Fools do not know this as it truly is, and only at the time of parinirvāṇa do they conceive the notion of extinction, saying:
'I and what belongs to me are now extinguished.'"

"Because they cling to a self and sentient beings—and so forth, as extensively explained, up to—knowers and seers, and because they cling to the notion that phenomena which lack intrinsic nature are utterly extinguished at the time of parinirvāṇa, I say that such individuals are all unable to be liberated from birth, old age, death, sorrow, lamentation, suffering, grief, and despair."

Why is this so? Because those of a deluded nature neither know nor awaken to the fundamental nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*). Due to their lack of knowledge and awakening regarding the fundamental nature of phenomena, they constantly contend with the Buddha, the World-Honored One, the great disciples, and the non-retrogressive bodhisattvas—who possess profound faith and understanding in the most profound Dharma, who always delight in practicing the conduct of non-apprehension (*anupalambha*), who have planted various roots of goodness under past Buddhas, who possess great supernormal powers and great influence, and who are true, pure caravan leaders and unsurpassed celestial seers.

Because of their contentious disputes, those foolish people sink for a long night into impurity, stench, and filth; all the worthy and holy ones avoid them from afar, and wise men together revile and loathe the cycle of birth and death as base and evil.
Just as near a city, town, or village, the manure and soil increase in impurity, loathsomeness, and foul odors of excrement and urine as people and animals come and go day and night;

so too, the foolish person, being unable to awaken to the fundamental nature of phenomena, increases the most evil, stinking, putrid, and impure cycle of birth and death, which is censured by the noble ones and shunned by the wise. I say that such a person cannot be liberated from the various afflictions of birth, old age, sickness, and so forth.
Then, Nāgaśrī asked: "Venerable One!
How is it that one can know phenomena as they truly are?"
Mañjuśrī said:
"All those who, with a non-conceptual mind, accord with seclusion, incline toward seclusion, and arrive at seclusion—such persons are able to know phenomena as they truly are."
Nāgaśrī said: "Who is able to distance themselves from illusory phenomena?
Mañjuśrī replied:
"Thus, this very [mind] is able to remain detached from illusory phenomena.
At that time, Subhūti arrived at their location and asked,
"What were you two great beings discussing?"
Then, Mañjuśrī questioned him, saying:
"Venerable One!
What dharma do you now describe as being called a 'Great Being'?"

We do not see even the slightest real dharma that could be called a "Great Being" (Mahāsattva) for us to discuss together; nor has the Great Holy Dharma-King ever said that there is even the slightest real dharma named a "Great Being."
"All phenomena are like echoes and are not at all real; how could an echo possibly engage in discourse?

Having heard these words, the Venerable Subhūti entered the samādhi-door of non-apprehension. After a brief moment, he arose from that concentration and, with palms joined in reverence toward the Jeta Grove, spoke thus:

"I now take refuge in what the Buddha has realized and taught—it is all exceedingly profound, subtle, and tranquil; difficult to see and difficult to awaken to; beyond the reach of discursive thought and transcending the sphere of thought; forever destroying grasping and severing all fetters and bonds. Such a wondrous Dharma is inconceivable, bringing benefit and happiness to all sentient beings who hear it."

If there are bodhisattvas who have already attained non-retrogression, with Mañjuśrī as their leader, down to those bodhisattvas who have first resolved their minds toward great enlightenment, they all together engage in this profound Dharma, conversing with one another in mutual intimacy.
Mañjuśrī said: "Virtuous One!
You should know that herein there is neither kin nor stranger, neither delusion nor non-delusion, and furthermore, there is no mutual discourse among one another."
Why is this so? Because there is not even the slightest dharma that can act as a friend, an enemy, or anything else toward another dharma.
For what reason?
"Because all phenomena are non-existent.
The Venerable Subhūti spoke again:
"Just now we saw two Great Beings discussing the profound Dharma; how can you say there is no matter for discussion?"
Mañjuśrī said: "Venerable sir,

have you ever heard of an illusory being, a dream-vision, an echo, a reflection, a mirage, a shadow, a transformation, or a city of Gandharvas discussing the profound meaning of the Dharma with one another?"
He replied, "No. Mañjuśrī said:
"All phenomena are like illusions, dream-visions, echoes, and so forth; how can it be said that they see one another and engage in discourse?
Could an illusory person hear the profound meaning of the Dharma spoken by an emanated Buddha, and then believe, understand, receive, uphold, or engage in conceptualizing names, phrases, and so on?"
At that time, having heard these words, Subhūti entered the meditative absorption of cessation at that very spot.
Then, Śāriputra came to that place and asked Mañjuśrī:
"O Great Being!"
"Do you know what kind of meditative concentration the Honored One has entered now?
Mañjuśrī replied, "Yes, I do."

Śāriputra! The venerable Subhūti does not contradict even the slightest dharma; by virtue of this, he constantly enters the concentration of non-contradiction, the concentration of non-abiding, the concentration of non-reliance on dharmas, the concentration of non-appropriation, and the concentration of destroying appropriation.
It is not that within this state there is speaking or discourse, coming or going, staying or lying down.
Why is this? Because, Venerable Subhūti, you have faith and understanding that the intrinsic nature of all phenomena is empty and unapprehendable.
At that time, Śāriputra asked again:
"What is the nature of all phenomena?
Mañjuśrī replied:
"All phenomena have non-existence as their nature; even such non-existence cannot be apprehended.
At that moment, Subhūti arose from his meditative absorption.
Mañjuśrī said:
"The time for the meal is approaching; you should enter the city quickly to wander for alms.
Subhūti replied, "Great Being, you should know this!"
I shall no longer enter the city to beg for alms. Why is this?

I have already distanced myself from all notions of cities, towns, villages, and the like; I have also distanced myself from all notions of forms, sounds, odors, tastes, tangibles, and mental phenomena.
Mañjuśrī said: "Venerable Subhūti!
If one has already become detached from all conceptualizations, how can there currently be the act of wandering and coming and going?"
Subhūti questioned him, saying:

"How is it that a transformation created by the Tathāgata manifests the various dharmas such as form, feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness? How does it manifest walking, coming and going, bending and stretching, and looking around?"
Mañjuśrī said: "Excellent! Excellent!"
"Venerable Subhūti!
You are a true son of the Buddha; therefore, the Tathāgata has always said:
'Subhūti is foremost among those who dwell in the state of non-contention.'"
He spoke again:
"Venerable sir!
Let us set this matter aside for now; I wish to enter the city to wander for alms, and once the meal is finished, I shall go to where the Tathāgata is."
"I shall invite these great virtuous ones and provide them with rare food so that they may obtain excellent benefit.
Śāriputra said, "Great Being!"
"What kind of food do you wish to provide for us now?
Mañjuśrī replied,
"Virtuous ones!..."

The food I have now prepared cannot be divided into portions, nor can it be swallowed; it is neither fragrance, taste, nor touch, nor is it subsumed within the three realms, yet it is not unconditioned either.
"Venerable sir, you should know that such sublime food is the food of the Tathāgata,
not any other food! Śāriputra said:
"Now that we have heard the Great Being speak the names of these rare foods, we are all already fully satiated; how much more so were we to actually receive them!
Mañjuśrī said, "As for this food of mine, neither flesh-eyes, divine eyes, nor the eye of wisdom can see it."
At that time, upon hearing these words, Subhūti and Śāriputra both entered the meditative absorption of cessation (nirodhasamāpatti).
Then, the Bodhisattva Sucintita asked Mañjuśrī,
"What food do these two superior persons consume now, and into what meditative absorption have they entered?"
Mañjuśrī said:
"These two venerable ones consume the untainted food (anāhāra) and enter a meditative absorption that is without support and free from defilement.
All who eat this food and abide in this absorption shall ultimately never again consume the food of the three realms."

At that time, Subhūti and Śāriputra both arose from their meditative absorption. Together with Mañjuśrī, the various bodhisattvas, śrāvakas, and the rest of the assembly, they mutually offered greetings of joy and consolation. Each then entered the city and wandered about for alms as they pleased.
The Venerable Subhūti entered a certain house that was empty and quiet and remained there in silence; a female lay follower, having seen him, asked:
"Venerable One!..."
"Abiding here, what do you desire? Subhūti replied,
"Sisters, you should know this!"
"I have come to stay here for the sake of begging for alms.
The female lay follower said,
"Noble Subhūti!"
"Have you not yet fully understood the perception of food?
Subhūti replied,
"From the very beginningless limit, I have already fully understood all perceptions of food."
"Why is that? Because all perceptions of food—its beginning, middle, and end—are naturally empty.
The female lay follower said:
“Certainly! Noble One, please extend your hand yourself; I shall offer you food.”
The Venerable Subhūti then extended his hand.
The female lay devotee said:
"Noble Subhūti!..."
"Is this now the hand of an Arhat?
Subhūti replied,
"The hand of an Arhat cannot be seen, nor can it be extended."
Sisters, you should know this: it is like a conjured being asking another conjured being, "What is called the hand of a conjured being? I now wish to see it; please extend it for me.
Sisters, you should know!
"Does that illusory person's hand have any capacity for seeing or can it be extended?
The female lay follower replied, "No!"
"Venerable One!
Subhūti replied, "It is so!"
"Sisters!
Because the Buddha has taught that all things are like illusions and are empty, one cannot say that the Arhat’s hand truly exists, can be seen, or can be extended.

When those women heard this teaching, they immediately could no longer see Subhūti’s hand; consequently, after a long time had passed, they were unable to offer him food, and when they wished to place it in his bowl, the bowl likewise disappeared.

That upāsikā circumambulated the body of Subhūti, searching for his hand all around, yet she could not find it; in the space of a single instant, his body had vanished. She then paid homage and praised Subhūti, saying:
"Excellent! Excellent!"
Excellent!
Noble One! Noble One!
That you are thus able to neither abide in this body nor manifest any marks is truly rare; for this reason, the Tathāgata has always said:
"Subhūti’s attainment of the dwelling in non-contention is the most supreme."
At that moment, the female lay follower immediately severed her view of a self at that very spot and attained the fruit of stream-entry.
The Venerable Subhūti then manifested his presence and praised her, saying:
"Excellent!"
Excellent, sisters!
You have thus been able to accomplish the deeds of a man.
At that time, the woman was filled with joy and leaped for gladness; she offered the food she had brought to Subhūti. Having accepted it, Subhūti went out and ate it upon his return.

Then, after Mañjuśrī and the assembly of bodhisattvas and śrāvakas had each finished their meal, they all proceeded together to where the Buddha was. They prostrated at his feet, circumambulated him three times to the right, and withdrew to sit at one side, reporting the aforementioned matter in detail to the World-Honored One.
At that time, having heard what he had related, the Tathāgata immediately praised him, saying:
"Excellent! Excellent!"
"You have been able to accomplish this sublime feat; you should know that it is entirely due to the Buddha’s spiritual power.

The Venerable Subhūti also informed the Buddha of how he had led the female lay follower who had undergone conversion to attain the first fruit. At that time, the World-Honored One likewise praised her skillful means.
Then, Mañjuśrī said to Subhūti:
"The view of self that was severed by that upāsikā was not actually a view of self; therefore, the Tathāgata calls it 'the view of self.'"
In this way, Venerable One!
All those who have set out upon the Bodhisattva vehicle should know, see, and have deep faith and understanding regarding all phenomena.
What is faith-understanding?
It means not abiding in conceptualization in accordance with the Dharma. Why is this so?
"Venerable Subhūti!
That which is called the 'concept of dharmas' is itself not a concept of dharmas; therefore, the Tathāgata refers to it by the name 'concept of dharmas.
Venerable one, you should know this!"

If a bodhisattva-mahāsattva were to fill countless worlds with the seven treasures and offer them as a gift, and if a son or daughter of good family were to receive, uphold, and even teach a single four-line verse of this Prajñāpāramitā to others while remaining free from the notion of teaching—it would be superior [to the former].
"The mass of merit obtained by these sons and daughters of good family is far greater than the former.
At that time, the World-Honored One spoke in verse:
"Like stars, an optical illusion, a lamp, a phantom, Dew, a bubble, a dream, lightning, and a cloud,"
"Regarding all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛta*), one should maintain such a contemplation.

Then, when the Bhagavān had finished speaking this sutra, all the bodhisattvas and bhikṣus, as well as the entire assembly—including gods, humans, asuras, and others—having heard what the Buddha taught, were filled with great joy; they accepted it with faith and practiced accordingly.
The Great Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra, Fascicle Five Hundred and Seventy-Six.
